lead: A single transistor biased in class A burns current even in silence. A push-pull stage splits the work: one transistor carries the positive half-cycle, a second carries the negative half. Each rests for half the cycle, so the stage draws almost no supply current at idle and reaches a theoretical efficiency of 78.5 %. Class B does this but leaves a flat spot near zero volts, called crossover distortion. Class AB biases both transistors slightly on, spending a little idle current to remove that flat spot. Radio, TV and phone audio power stages use this idea.
prereq: You need: class A and class B conduction angles and efficiency from Chapter 3.5, and the complementary emitter follower from Unit 2, Transistor Biasing and Small-Signal Amplifiers.

blocks.text: Class B means a device conducts for 180°, exactly half a cycle. A push-pull stage gives each half to its own transistor: one for the positive swing, one for the negative. With zero input both are off, so the stage draws no supply current. A class A stage, by contrast, burns current even in silence.

In the transformer-coupled form, an input transformer with a centre-tapped secondary feeds antiphase base drives to two NPN transistors. Their emitters are grounded and their collectors drive the two halves of an output transformer primary. The output transformer adds the half-sine waves back into a full sine. The load gets no DC, but transformers are heavy and block low frequencies.

The transformerless form is what real equipment uses, called OTL (output transformer-less). An NPN and a PNP sit in complementary symmetry as emitter followers, emitters joined at the output node, fed from +Vcc and −Vcc. The NPN sources current into RL on the positive half; the PNP sinks current on the negative half. A single supply with a large output coupling capacitor also works, and a bridge (BTL) connection doubles the swing.

When good power PNPs were hard to make, designers used quasi-complementary output: two NPN power devices, the lower one in Darlington with a PNP driver, so it behaves like a PNP. Modern devices make true complementary pairs normal.
Class A push-pull is the alternative: both transistors conduct all the time, there is no dead zone, but the best efficiency is 50 % against 78.5 % for class B.
Assume the output swings to the supply rail, ignoring V_CE(sat). Then the peak output voltage is V_peak = Vcc and the peak output current is I_peak = Vcc/RL.

blocks.where: Vcc is the magnitude of each supply in volts, RL is the load resistance in ohms, and P_out(max) is the largest sine-wave power delivered to the load in watts.
I_dc is the average current one supply delivers over a full cycle in amperes; each supply passes a half-sine once per cycle, whose average over the full period is I_peak/π.
P_DC is the total DC power taken from both supplies in watts. The factor 2 appears because the positive half comes from the +Vcc rail and the negative half from the −Vcc rail, and both carry current.
η is the conversion efficiency, the fraction of DC power turned into signal power.

blocks.text: 78.5 % is a ceiling, reached only at full drive. At a smaller swing V_peak the output power falls as V_peak² but the DC power falls only as V_peak, so η = (π/4)(V_peak/Vcc) drops quickly. Quiet passages of music run at low efficiency even in a class B stage.

sections.h3: Crossover distortion, and how class AB removes it

blocks.text: A silicon BJT stays off until its base-emitter voltage reaches about 0.7 V. At the zero crossing the input must rise 0.7 V before the NPN turns on, and fall 0.7 V before the PNP turns on. The output therefore has a flat step of about ±0.7 V around zero. That flat spot is crossover distortion. It is worst for quiet signals, looks like a kink in the sine wave, and adds odd harmonics (see Chapter 3.8).

Class AB fixes it by biasing the two bases apart by roughly 2V_BE, about 1.4 V, so both devices idle at a small quiescent current I_Q of a few mA to tens of mA. There are two bias circuits. Two forward-biased diodes give about 1.4 V. A V_BE multiplier uses one transistor with a base divider R1, R2 to give V_BB = V_BE(1 + R1/R2); it is adjustable and can be mounted on the heat sink so the bias falls as the output devices heat up.

The cost is idle dissipation, roughly P_Q = 2Vcc I_Q on a split supply. Small emitter resistors of 0.1 Ω to 0.47 Ω in series with each emitter steady the quiescent current against device mismatch and thermal runaway.
Each device now conducts for more than 180° but less than 360°, so efficiency lies between 50 % and 78.5 %, typically 60 % to 70 % in a well-set-up audio stage.

figure.caption: The phase splitter sends each half-cycle to its own transistor. Near zero volts both are cut off, and the dashed path marks the dead zone that flattens the output and causes crossover distortion.

spec.aria: Push-pull stage: the phase splitter drives an NPN for positive half-cycles and a PNP for negative half-cycles; near zero both are off, giving a dead zone and crossover distortion.

examples.question: A complementary (OTL) class B push-pull amplifier runs from ±12 V supplies into an 8 Ω loudspeaker. Find (a) the peak output voltage and current, (b) the maximum output power, (c) the DC power drawn from the supplies at full swing, (d) the conversion efficiency, and (e) the power dissipated in each output transistor at full swing.
steps: The output can swing to the rail, so V_peak = Vcc = 12 V. Peak current I_peak = V_peak/RL = 12/8 = 1.5 A.
Maximum output power P_out = Vcc²/(2RL) = 144/16 = 9 W. Check with rms values: V_rms = 12/√2 = 8.485 V, I_rms = 8.485/8 = 1.061 A, and 8.485 × 1.061 = 9 W.
Average current from one supply: I_dc = I_peak/π = 1.5/3.1416 = 0.477 A.
Two supplies feed the stage, so P_DC = 2 × Vcc × I_dc = 2 × 12 × 0.477 = 11.46 W. The formula gives the same: 2Vcc²/(πRL) = 288/25.13 = 11.46 W.
Efficiency η = P_out/P_DC = 9/11.46 = 0.785 = 78.5 %, the theoretical π/4.

The difference 11.46 − 9 = 2.46 W is dissipated by the two output devices, so 1.23 W each at full swing. This is not the worst case; dissipation per device peaks at a lower drive, near V_peak = 2Vcc/π.
examples.answer: P_out(max) = 9 W, P_DC = 11.46 W, η = 78.5 %, and each transistor dissipates 1.23 W at full swing.
examples.check:
import math
Vcc = 12.0
RL = 8.0
Vp = Vcc
Ip = Vp / RL
Pout = Vcc**2 / (2 * RL)
Idc = Ip / math.pi
PDC = 2 * Vcc * Idc
eta = Pout / PDC * 100
Pd = (PDC - Pout) / 2
print(round(Pout, 2))
print(round(PDC, 2))
print(round(eta, 1))
print(round(Ip, 2))
print(round(Pd, 2))

traps: Using Vcc²/(πRL) for the DC power forgets that both supplies deliver current; the class B value is 2Vcc²/(πRL).
Putting the rms voltage into P = V²/(2RL): the formula already handles the rms conversion, so Vcc must be the peak (rail) value, 12 V and not 8.485 V.
Quoting 78.5 % as the efficiency at every volume. It is the ceiling at full swing; efficiency falls as drive falls, following η = (π/4)(V_peak/Vcc).
Assuming full-swing dissipation is the worst case for the transistors. Each device's dissipation peaks near V_peak = 2Vcc/π, well below the rail, and that peak sets the heat sink.
Calling class AB a class A circuit. Class AB conducts more than 180° but less than 360°, and its output is still push-pull.

quiz.q: What fraction of a cycle does each transistor conduct in a class B push-pull stage, and what is the maximum theoretical efficiency?
quiz.a: 180°, half a cycle each. Maximum efficiency is π/4 = 78.5 %.

quiz.q: Define crossover distortion and state its cause.
quiz.a: A flat step of about ±0.7 V in the output around the zero crossing, because each transistor stays cut off until its base-emitter voltage reaches the 0.7 V knee.

quiz.q: Why is the DC input power of a class B stage 2Vcc²/(πRL) and not Vcc²/(πRL)?
quiz.a: The positive half-cycle is supplied by the +Vcc rail and the negative half by the −Vcc rail. Each rail delivers an average current I_peak/π, so the two together give 2Vcc I_peak/π = 2Vcc²/(πRL).

quiz.q: How does a V_BE multiplier bias a class AB output stage, and why is it mounted on the heat sink?
quiz.a: It sets V_BB = V_BE(1 + R1/R2) between the two bases, holding a few mA of quiescent current. Thermal tracking lowers the bias as the devices heat, preventing thermal runaway of the quiescent current.

quiz.q: A class B push-pull stage runs from ±15 V supplies into a 4 Ω load. Find P_out(max), the DC input power at full swing, and the efficiency.
A push-pull amplifier's output shows a kink at the zero crossing that is relatively worse at low volume. Give the cause and two fixes.
quiz.a: Crossover distortion from the 0.7 V dead zone; it is a fixed voltage step, so it is a larger fraction of a small signal. Fixes: bias the stage into class AB using diodes or a V_BE multiplier, and add small emitter resistors to stabilise the quiescent current.

quiz.q: Why is a class AB stage less efficient than a class B stage even at full drive?
quiz.a: The bias holds a quiescent current I_Q flowing through both devices at all times, drawing extra DC power of about 2Vcc I_Q that produces no signal output. The loss is small when I_Q is a few mA but grows with the bias.

beyond: Not for the exam. In real audio design the bias spreader is the part that decides sound quality and reliability, so IC datasheets spend pages on it. Phone speakers and Bluetooth boxes now use class D switching stages, but class AB still rules low-cost line-powered audio and the output stage inside many op-amps. Thermal tracking of the V_BE multiplier, OTL versus BTL output coupling, and measurement of the crossover kink on a scope are the practical skills here. Search terms: class AB bias spreader, V_BE multiplier thermal tracking, OTL and BTL output stages, crossover distortion measurement.
